newsitem.title: GERMANY: German chemical sector restarts low-wage talks.
newsitem.headline: German chemical sector restarts low-wage talks.

text.p: Talks aimed at allowing employers in underperforming sectors of the German chemical industry to introduce special low-wage agreements for staff restarted in Frankfurt on Monday.

Employer negotiators are seeking separate wage pacts for workers in the plastics processing, chemical fibres and rubber processing sectors, which they say have been hit hard by weak economic conditions.

Union officials have said they are willing to discuss possible wage reductions as long as any new accords are coupled to job creation and protection measures. Entering the talks on Monday, they said negotiations were likely to be tough.
"Everything is open at the moment," one union official said.
Employers in Germany's large chemical industry have for some time been demanding the option to free wages in certain sectors from industry-wide agreements.
Some large firms, including tyre-maker Continental AG, have threatened to walk out of collective wage bargaining talks and negotiate their own deals if a low-wage agreement could not be reached.
Under a new proposal put forward by the chemical sector trade union IG Chemie, employers will be able to set "income corridors" within which wages could be determined.
The proposed model would also require firms to pay their employees bonuses during times of an upswing.

Germany's chemicals groups employ something over half a million workers. That figure has remained largely constant over the last year following a deal between employers and unions to maintain employment levels at mid-1996 levels.
But employer representatives signalled in January that increased consolidation in the sector meant they could no longer resist the mounting pressure to cut jobs this year.

Union and employer negotiators last December agreed a 1997 wage rise of 1.5 percent and decided not to enforce a new federal law allowing sick pay entitlements to be cut from the full 100 percent of salary to 80 percent.
